stem: Who was the first Portuguese Viceroy in India?
expl: Vasco da Gama was the first Portuguese to reach India. He arrived at the port of Calicut on the western coast of India on 20 May, 1498. By reaching here, he discovered a new sea route to India. The then ruler of Calicut, the Zamorin (Zamorin was the hereditary title of the rulers of Calicut), welcomed Vasco da Gama. Portuguese traders established their trading factories at the ports of Calicut, Goa, Daman, Diu and Hooghly in India. In 1505, Francisco de Almeida came to India as the first Portuguese Viceroy and Governor. In the context of commercial interests, to establish supremacy in the Indian Ocean, Almeida propounded the ‘Blue Water Policy’, i.e., the policy of dominance over the seas.

stem: Where in India did the British set up their first factory in 1613?
expl: Captain William Hawkins reached the Mughal court from Surat in April, 1609, but he could not succeed in obtaining permission to establish a factory at Surat. In 1611, despite Portuguese opposition, Captain Henry Middleton reached Swally (near Surat) and succeeded in obtaining permission from the Mughal governor to trade there. In 1612, Captain Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese at Swally (near Surat) and ended the continuation of their monopoly. After this, with Jahangir’s permission, the English permanently established a factory at Surat in 1613. It is noteworthy that the English had earlier set up their first factory (temporarily) at Masulipatnam. From here, the English expanded their trade to other parts of the country and soon established subsidiary factories at Ahmedabad, Burhanpur, Ajmer and Agra.

stem: Which one of the following was the immediate cause of the First Carnatic War?

options.label: d
options.text: Capture of French ships by the British

expl: The First Carnatic War (1746-48) was merely an extension of the War of the Austrian Succession, which began in 1740. Even against the orders of their home governments, war between the two parties (English and French) began in 1746. The immediate cause of the war was the seizure of some French ships by the English navy under Commodore Curtis Barnett. During the First Carnatic War itself, the Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin, sent an army under Mahfuz Khan to attack the French. Under Captain Paradis, the French army defeated the Nawab at a place called St. Thomé, situated on the Adyar River. With the end of war in Europe, the First Carnatic War also came to an end. By the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748), the War of the Austrian Succession ended, and Madras was restored to the English. The First Carnatic War is remembered for the Battle of St. Thomé.

stem: What was the main economic basis of the triangular trade between India, China, and England?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: The main basis of trade between India, China, and England was opium, tea, and cloth. The British East India Company established a monopoly over opium cultivation in regions such as Bengal and Bihar, compelled Indian farmers to cultivate opium, and exported it to China to reduce the trade imbalance. Britain needed tea, porcelain (crockery) and silk from China in large quantities. Therefore, as per the options, opium was the main economic basis of this trade.

stem: Which treaty was signed after the Battle of Buxar?
expl: The Battle of Buxar (October 1764) was fought between the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula, and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, on one side, and the British, on the other. The British won the battle. The British army was led by Hector Munro. After the end of this battle, two Treaties of Allahabad (1765) were concluded. The first Treaty of Allahabad was between Clive and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, while the second Treaty of Allahabad was between Clive and the Nawab of Awadh, Shuja-ud-Daula.

stem: Who was appointed Deputy Diwan of Murshidabad by Robert Clive after the Allahabad Treaty?
expl: According to the second Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765), the then-fugitive Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under British protection and kept at Allahabad. By his farman (royal order) dated 12 August 1765, Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa (present-day Odisha) permanently. In return, the Company would pay the Emperor 26 lakh rupees and would provide 53 lakh rupees for the expenses of the Nizamat. At this time, the Company neither wanted to take direct responsibility for revenue collection nor did it have such capacity. For the Diwani work, the Company appointed two Deputy Diwans—Muhammad Raza Khan for Murshidabad (Bengal) and Raja Shitab Rai for Bihar. Muhammad Raza Khan also worked as the Deputy Nazim. Thus, the entire Diwani and Nizamat administration continued to be run by Indians, although the responsibility rested with the Company.

stem: Emperor Shah Alam- II gave the Diwani of Bengal - Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company on:
expl: Under the First Treaty of Allahabad (12 August 1765), the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II permanently granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; and under the Second Treaty of Allahabad (16 August 1765), the Nawab of Awadh (Shuja-ud-Daula) promised to give the districts of Allahabad and Kara to the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. At this time, Robert Clive was the Governor of Bengal on behalf of the East India Company. The entire life of Shah Alam II was full of calamities. He was blinded in 1788. During the time of Shah Alam II, the British gained control over Delhi in 1803. Shah Alam II and his two successors Akbar II (1806–37) and Bahadur Shah II (1837–57) remained merely pensioners of the East India Company.

stem: The dual system of governance in Bengal was enforced by :

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: The Dual Government began in Bengal in 1765 during the time of Robert Clive. On 28 August 1772, the Court of Directors decided to abolish the Dual Government in Bengal. Warren Hastings implemented this decision in 1772. The Calcutta Council and its head were instructed to become the Diwan themselves and take the management of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa into their own hands. Warren Hastings removed both the Deputy-Diwans, Muhammad Raza Khan and Raja Shitab Rai.
